narrative:
The model estimated an 82.1% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, and that is why your law school application was rejected.

The denial was driven mainly by your class standing. Your third-year class rank was the single most influential factor: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and showed the same pattern—lowest decile versus an accepted-student average near the sixth decile—also pushing toward failure. Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most influential factor. Although it is below the accepted-student average of 37.18, its influence in the model pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the two class-rank signals.

To move forward, ask admissions for feedback on your file, consider retaking the LSAT only if practice scores show meaningful improvement, and seek additional rigorous coursework or academic preparation that demonstrates readiness for law study. Reapply only when you can present stronger evidence of likely bar success.
